newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Swiss Holocaust fund plan weighs on gold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss Holocaust fund plan weighs on gold.

text.p: Gold prices fell on Wednesday as a proposal that Switzerland sell gold from its reserves to establish a memorial fund for Holocaust victims came on top of dwindling confidence about the market's strength, dealers said.
Gold was fixed at $354.50 an ounce in the afternoon from $355.75 earlier and well down on on Monday's $362.15, its highest fixing since January 3.
New York markets were also sharply lower, citing the Swiss proposal as an additional factor in depressing already weakening trade.
As recently as February 12 gold fixed at a 3-3/4 year low of $336.90 before bouncing back.

Swiss President Arnold Koller earlier proposed that a memorial foundation be established for victims of the Holocaust and other tragedies. Its capital fund of about seven billion Swiss francs ($4.7 billion) would be raised through selling revalued Swiss gold reserves.
This would entail selling gold over a 10-year period, according to Swiss National bank chairman Hans Meyer.
Some analysts translated that as meaning Switzerland would sell about 40 tonnes of gold a year to capitalise the fund.
Meyer told a news conference that sales would not disrupt the gold market and had no implications for the stability of the Swiss franc.

Ted Arnold, metals market analyst at Merrill Lynch, described the tonnage as "a drop in the ocean" for a market that has a daily turnover of around 900 tonnes, according to data from the London Bullion Market Association.
"The amount is not huge by any means but it is indicative of central bank sentiment towards the market," one senior bullion dealer said.

Gold prices began to weaken late last year on concerns that European central banks would mobilise their gold reserves as part of their strategy to meet the economic criteria for joining a European single currency in 1999.
Rumours of national bank sales swept the market, wrecking sentiment and taking prices to February's low.
The previous month, the Dutch central bank announced it had sold 300 tonnes from its reserves. But when no further similar announcements followed, sentiment began to revive.

Investment funds which had built huge short positions -- selling gold they did not own on the expectation of being able to buy it back at a lower price later -- were forced to start covering those positions and the price began to rise.
"The market turned bullish on the fact that there were no more central bank sales. Now the Swiss news has turned it again," said Arnold.
However, some dealers conceded that at recent levels above $360.00, the gold price was beginning to look "toppy".
"Gold had a short-covering rally and now that that is over we could see the lows again," one dealer said.

Legislation necessary to allow the Swiss move would take about two years, according to Meyer. Swiss gold reserves are valued currently at 4,595 Swiss francs a kg and would need to be revalued by almost four times to meet present market value.
"On the basis of a more realistic -- albeit still cautious -- valuation, several billion francs could be transferred in gold to the foundation," Meyer said.
Late last year gold market confidence slumped on another proposal from Switzerland that it begin the process of ending the need to have 40 percent of its note issue backed with gold.
Silver prices held unchanged at $5.25, down a cent but there were losses in platinum and palladium.

Since platinum raced last week to more than $400 and palladium to $157 following Russia's failure to begin export contract talks with Japan for this year and a threatened strike at Russia's Norilsk, the prices have fallen steadily.
"Talk of Japanese users substituting nickel for palladium in some applications has got people a bit nervy and others are taking profits after a good run," said one dealer.
Platinum was at $379.00/$380.00 down $6.00 and palladium $143.5044.50, down $6.50. ($ = 1.485 Swiss Francs)
